claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a reported hierarchical heterostructure with multilevel chemical fluctuations.
A physics-informed machine-learning model combining microstructural descriptors with reduced-order finite-element analyses can predict Young’s modulus of hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed hybrid model can predict the yield strength of hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed hybrid model can predict the toughness of hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
Reduced-order finite-element models can capture stress distributions and crack initiation sufficiently for training the surrogate.
Quantitative microstructural descriptors can be extracted from imaging and compositional analyses for use in the surrogate model.
The distribution and connectivity of chemically fluctuating regions are meaningful descriptors of material behavior.
Interphase or interface boundaries in the hierarchical heterostructure mediate load transfer.
The hierarchical features control local stress concentrations relevant to deformation and fracture.
Linking descriptors of structural heterogeneity to simplified physics simulations permits interpolation of elastic response.
The same descriptor-and-simulation framework permits interpolation of plastic response and crack initiation.
The reduced-order surrogate bypasses exhaustive high-fidelity computations while retaining relevant micromechanical physics.
The model will reduce prediction error for Young’s modulus, yield strength, and toughness by roughly 50% relative to the stated baseline methods.
The model will lower computational cost by approximately 80% relative to the stated baseline methods.
Thermophysical calculations, CALPHAD, and full-scale first-principles or DFT methods are computationally demanding and inefficient for predicting fracture properties.
The approach may become unreliable if its descriptors omit critical deformation or fracture mechanisms.
The approach may become unreliable if its calibration simulations do not span the local heterogeneity encountered under extreme loading.
Model predictions can be benchmarked against tensile and standardized fracture measurements from the same specimen batch.

Failure to achieve at least a 50% reduction in mean absolute prediction error, approximately 80% lower computational cost, or toughness and fracture-initiation predictions within the specified tolerances would falsify the hypothesis.
